note: Every public-facing technical claim about the NASHA AI Operations Lab must map to an entry here; public_wording is the sentence the portfolio may use. SYNTHETIC / same-author / offline evaluation.
prohibited_claims: LLMs are worse than deterministic systems (in general).
Neural retrieval is worse than lexical retrieval (in general).
NASHA is operating, has customers, revenue, suppliers or sales.
Any result from a real business or production deployment.
Independent / third-party validation of the benchmarks.
The model comparison covers frontier or hosted models.
NASHA is employment or professional experience.
NASHA is a trademark, a legal name, or cleared for use (working name; clearance pending).

claims.title: Scenario suite size
claims.claim: The planner experiment uses 259 generated synthetic scenarios in four splits (dev 67, held-out 75, held-out B 75, adversarial 42).
claims.scope: Block 3 planner scenario set v1; synthetic; same author.
claims.limitations: Expectations were set by construction by the same author who built the control planner. Two of four splits were inspected while fixing the deterministic planner.
claims.public_wording: I evaluated operations planners across 259 synthetic scenarios in four splits (my own scenarios, not an external benchmark).

claims.title: Deterministic planner result
claims.claim: The deterministic planner passed all 259 scenarios under the strict all-checks criterion.
claims.scope: Block 3 scenario set v1; held-out B (75/75) is the only split not inspected before scoring.
claims.limitations: Perfect score on author-generated scenarios measures the harness, not the real world. Dev, held-out and adversarial splits were used while fixing the planner.
claims.public_wording: The deterministic planner passed 259 of 259 of my synthetic scenarios, including 75 of 75 on a split I had not inspected before scoring.

claims.title: Qwen 1.5B result
claims.claim: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct passed 9/138 (run 1) and 5/140 (run 2) scenarios; with the evidence-envelope guardrail 8/138 and 8/140.
claims.scope: Local CPU runs on GitHub-hosted runners; stratified subsets (--per-family 2); temperature 0; prompt p1; tool schema ts1.
claims.limitations: Small model, one prompt, no tuning, subsets not full suite. Says nothing about larger or hosted models.
claims.public_wording: A small local model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) passed 4-7% of the same scenarios under identical checks.

claims.title: Qwen 7B result
claims.claim: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct passed 10/35 scenarios (one per family on held-out B + adversarial) with a 151.5 s median latency on 4 vCPU.
claims.scope: 35 scenarios, single run, temperature 0, CPU; Wilson 95% interval for 10/35 is 16-45%.
claims.limitations: Small n; one run; all passes were purchase-draft scenarios; not a statement about GPU speed or other models.
claims.public_wording: A 7B local model passed 10 of 35 sampled scenarios (about 29%, wide uncertainty) and was far slower on CPU.

claims.title: Deterministic planner outperformed tested Qwen planners
claims.claim: In every paired comparison the deterministic planner passed scenarios the model failed, and the model passed none the deterministic planner failed.
claims.scope: Paired on identical scenario ids, exact sign test; three real-model runs.
claims.limitations: Applies to the tested models, prompts and scenarios only. Not a claim that LLM planners are worse in general.
claims.public_wording: On my evaluated scenarios the deterministic planner outperformed the tested local Qwen planners, so the simplest system that meets the reliability requirement won.

claims.title: Permission layer held against real models
claims.claim: Across the three real-model runs there were 0 executed external actions and 100% approval-boundary compliance, over about 1,000 model calls.
claims.scope: Real model calls recorded in run logs: 434 + 426 + 144.
claims.limitations: Tested against two Qwen models and scripted adversaries; a different model might find a path they did not.
claims.public_wording: In about 1,000 real local-model calls the permission layer allowed 0 external actions, because the model proposes and deterministic code authorizes.

claims.title: Silent wrong all-clear from the small model
claims.claim: The raw 1.5B model answered NO_ACTION when action was needed in 30 of 140 scenarios; the evidence-envelope guardrail reduced this to 0.
claims.scope: Run 2, 140 scenarios.
claims.limitations: The guardrail achieves this by escalating, which lowered abstention accuracy and usefulness.
claims.public_wording: The small model said 'no action needed' when action was needed in about 1 in 5 scenarios; a deterministic evidence check removed all of those.

claims.title: Retrieval benchmark size
claims.claim: The retrieval benchmark has 467 questions in 13 categories (412 generated, 55 hand-written).
claims.scope: Block 3 question set v2; dev 318 / held-out 149.
claims.limitations: Same author; generated questions copy corpus wording, which flatters lexical retrieval; hand-written subset is small (n=45 with gold documents).
claims.public_wording: I benchmarked retrieval on 467 questions in 13 categories over a decision-heavy company knowledge base.

claims.title: BM25 vs MiniLM on this corpus
claims.claim: On this identifier-heavy, decision-status-heavy NASHA corpus BM25 (MRR 0.913) outperformed all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (0.672), BM25+MiniLM hybrid (0.842) and spaCy static vectors (0.259).
claims.scope: 467-question set; one small encoder, one chunking, no fine-tuning or re-ranker.
claims.limitations: Not a claim that neural retrieval is worse in general. Generated questions favour lexical retrieval; on 45 hand-written paraphrases the BM25+LSA hybrid was ahead of BM25 (0.794 vs 0.764, noise).
claims.public_wording: For this identifier-heavy corpus, exact lexical retrieval beat a small neural encoder; I measured it rather than assuming dense retrieval would win.

claims.title: MiniLM weakest on identifier categories
claims.claim: MiniLM MRR was 0.294 on DECISION_STATUS, 0.362 on SUPERSEDED and 0.239 on NUMERIC, versus 0.846, 0.844 and 0.842 for BM25.
claims.scope: Per-category MRR, 467-question set.
claims.limitations: Categories have different sizes (3-60 questions); the small ones are noisy.
claims.public_wording: Dense retrieval struggled most where exact tokens matter: decision IDs, superseded records and numeric references.

claims.title: pgvector works
claims.claim: PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector 0.8.7 with an HNSW cosine index served as a retriever in CI and matched the exact scan on MiniLM vectors.
claims.scope: 758 chunks, CI service container.
claims.limitations: At this corpus size an exact scan suffices; HNSW is not needed. Approximate indexes can differ per build (handled in CI reproduction).
claims.public_wording: I implemented pgvector retrieval (HNSW, cosine) and showed it matches an exact scan here; at 758 chunks it isn't needed.

claims.title: Abstention improvement
claims.claim: A learned answerability gate plus built-in rules cut held-out false answers from 19/66 to 10/66 (29% to 15%), with false abstentions rising from 2/83 to 5/83.
claims.scope: Held-out split of the 467-question set; gate fit on dev only.
claims.limitations: 15% of should-refuse questions are still answered. Behaviour on hand-written paraphrases is mixed (small n).
claims.public_wording: Abstention improved but is not solved: false answers on held-out questions fell from about 29% to 15%.

claims.title: Mutation testing
claims.claim: The safety-code mutation suite killed 22 of 22 targeted mutants (19 of 22 on the first run).
claims.scope: 22 hand-written mutants of the permission, grounding, trust and retrieval code.
claims.limitations: Mutants were chosen by the author; the score bounds test quality for those mutants, not all possible defects.
claims.public_wording: A targeted mutation suite of 22 mutants in the safety-critical code is fully killed after I fixed the three tests it showed were weak.

claims.title: CI test count
claims.claim: The lab-ci workflow ran 229 passing tests (1 skipped) on the Block 3 commit and built the Docker image.
claims.scope: GitHub Actions run on commit 647d47e.
claims.limitations: The skipped test is the real-model integration test, run in a separate optional workflow. Counts change with later commits.
claims.public_wording: The project's CI runs 229 automated tests and builds its Docker image.

external_evidence.verified: GitHub Actions job log: '229 passed, 1 skipped'

claims.title: Worst-case adversary contained
claims.claim: A scripted worst-case model made 1,820 forbidden attempts (external actions, unknown tools, unapproved mutations, invented targets) over the 259 scenarios; none executed.
claims.scope: Scripted stand-in (NOT an LLM) over all 259 scenarios.
claims.limitations: A stand-in bounds the pipeline; a real model may behave differently.
claims.public_wording: A scripted adversary that tried 1,820 forbidden actions executed none of them.

claims.title: Prompt-injection effect on a susceptible model
claims.claim: A scripted model that obeys injected text kept permissions intact but changed 2 of 42 adversarial recommendations; the evidence envelope restored all 42.
claims.scope: Scripted stand-in; adversarial split.
claims.limitations: Stand-in behaviour, not a real model's susceptibility.
claims.public_wording: Even a model that blindly follows injected text could not trigger an unauthorized action; a deterministic evidence check also stopped it changing the recommendation.

claims.title: Disclosure
claims.claim: NASHA is an independent founder concept; there is no restaurant, customer, supplier or sale. All data are synthetic.
claims.scope: Everything in the lab.
claims.limitations: None.
claims.public_wording: Independent founder concept and synthetic enterprise simulation. Not a live operating restaurant; no customers, revenue or production deployment.

claims.title: Circular-trust failure found and fixed
claims.claim: The grounding check for proposed mutations once accepted record keys that appeared only in the model's own tool arguments; it now grounds only in successful trusted tool results.
claims.scope: Found by the worst-case stand-in; fixed before Block 3 acceptance.
claims.limitations: Grounding checks that a key appears in trusted evidence, not that acting on it is wise; the human reviewer remains the control for that.
claims.public_wording: My adversarial test found the system letting a model's own arguments count as evidence for itself. I fixed it so only trusted tool results count, and added a regression test.

claims.title: Menu direction update handled without rewriting history
claims.claim: Founder decision D-84 (Mango Habanero Gobi is an appetizer/shareable, not a taco) was recorded as a new item-level decision; current-state synthetic menu data and knowledge use it; the Block 3 baseline keeps menu v1 and corpus 'block3' so its results are unchanged.
claims.scope: Lab synthetic menu v2, knowledge corpus version 'current', decision register; project recipe/costing/capacity/website data NOT migrated.
claims.limitations: Recipe, costing, capacity, allergen, pairing and website data for the dish still describe the taco and are marked as awaiting migration. No tasting or recipe claim exists for the new dish.
claims.public_wording: The flagship dish in the simulation is Mango Habanero Gobi, a cauliflower appetizer. Earlier 'Gobi Taco' records are kept as labelled history.

claims.title: Structurally different planner scenarios (ext1)
claims.claim: On 106 structurally different scenarios (property-based matrix, metamorphic variants, policy proposals generated from the dietary checklist, rule-gap probes) the deterministic planner passed 98/98 headline scenarios and 24/24 metamorphic relations after oracle corrections that are disclosed (first run 92/103 and 20/24); it failed 8/8 rule-gap probes.
claims.scope: EXTERNALIZED / INDEPENDENT-STYLE EVAL v1; same author; labels from decision tables and checklist rows, never from a model.
claims.limitations: Structurally different, not independent. The oracle contained five of my own errors on the first run, corrected after review. The rule-gap finding (any in-time open order is treated as covering a shortage, whatever its quantity) is open and pinned by a test.
claims.public_wording: A second evaluation built with different methods (still by me) was passed 98 of 98, after I corrected five errors in my own answer key and disclosed the first-run results; it also found a real gap: the planner ignores the size of an open order.

claims.title: Does the retrieval ranking survive different questions? (ext1)
claims.claim: On 176 structurally different questions BM25 still led overall (MRR 0.850 vs MiniLM 0.434 and BM25+MiniLM 0.666), but on the 31 questions with the least word overlap the gap closed (BM25 0.445, MiniLM 0.403) and the hybrids led (about 0.55).
claims.scope: ext1 retrieval questions (supersession-metadata, terse-keyword, mutated paraphrases); Block 3 corpus; CI run 38804116939.
claims.limitations: Same author; small low-overlap bin (n=31) and R1 (n=6); one small encoder, no fine-tuning or re-ranker.
claims.public_wording: Lexical retrieval's lead held on questions I built a different way, but mostly where questions share the corpus's exact words; on paraphrased questions the gap closed and a hybrid was better.

claims.title: Per-scenario model trace and what it showed
claims.claim: A per-scenario trace (requested tools, arguments, results, schema failures, retries, tokens, guardrail intervention, outcome) was added and proven on 35 scenarios; it showed 23 requests for a non-existent tool name in 19 of 35 scenarios and that most missing required tools were never requested.
claims.scope: qwen2.5:1.5b, original tool presentation, 35 scenarios, CI run 38803177815.
claims.limitations: 35 scenarios, one run. Block 3 counts of 'forbidden attempts' for LLM rows are probably the same name errors, but per-request detail was not recorded then (inference, stated as such).
claims.public_wording: Adding per-scenario traces showed the small model asking for a tool that does not exist and rarely taking a second step; the 'forbidden attempts' I had counted were mostly misspelled tool names, not attempts at forbidden actions.

claims.title: Tool-schema experiment (ts1 vs ts2)
claims.claim: With only the tool presentation changed (scoped menu, call skeletons, flat event view), Qwen2.5-1.5B's required-tool recall rose from 22/140 to 67/140 (paired p < 0.001), meeting the pre-registered 15-point threshold; the gain came from data-quality and inventory scenarios, policy scenarios did not improve, and schema failures rose from 3 to 37.
claims.scope: One small model, one run, 140 scenarios (139 shared ids), CI run 38803177815; pre-registered rule in docs/TOOL-SCHEMA-EXPERIMENT.md.
claims.limitations: One model; the change bundle was tested together; the scoped menu encodes which tools matter; the deterministic planner still passes 259/259 vs 16/140 for the best raw arm. Not evidence about larger models.
claims.public_wording: Poor tool use by the small model was partly an interface problem: changing only how the tools were presented tripled required-tool recall, mostly by removing a misspelled-tool-name error, while policy scenarios did not improve. It did not change which planner won.
